finding.claim: Unauthenticated SSRF: the POST parameter `feed` is passed straight to file_get_contents(), so any visitor can make the server fetch arbitrary URLs. This includes internal hosts, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) and non-HTTP wrappers such as file://, php://, phar://, ftp:// and gopher-style schemes. The response is only partly visible: the handler echoes strlen() of the body. That gives a size oracle, an internal port/host probe via timing and error behaviour, and blind request triggering.
finding.source: $_POST['feed'] (import.php:11-12), attacker-controlled HTTP POST body, no authentication required

trace.note: Branch is entered for any POST request with a `feed` field. There is no require_admin() call and no session check on this path.
$_POST['feed'] is passed unmodified to file_get_contents(), which honours http(s), ftp, file, php:// and phar:// stream wrappers, and follows HTTP redirects.
strlen($xml) is echoed back to the attacker, leaking the response size. This allows content-length probing of internal resources and confirms whether a file or URL exists.

finding.guards_checked: No scheme allowlist, host allowlist, DNS or IP resolution check, private-range blocklist or redirect restriction. require_admin() exists but is not called on this path. The only guard in the file is the session-based admin check, and it covers only the set_webhook branch. Whether allow_url_fopen is disabled in php.ini was not checked; it defaults to On.

verdict.reason: import.php:11-13 lets any POST with `feed` reach file_get_contents($_POST['feed']) at line 12 with no auth, since require_admin() is only called at line 18, and echoes strlen() at line 13; there is no scheme or host validation anywhere in the file.

finding.claim: SSRF via the admin-only webhook setter: `set_webhook` is passed directly to curl_init() and curl_exec() with no validation, so an admin (or anyone who obtains an admin session) can make the server request arbitrary internal URLs. The curl handle has no CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS restriction, so file://, gopher://, dict:// and similar schemes work. Redirects are not followed by default, because CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is unset. The response is not echoed, so this is blind SSRF. The admin gate lowers severity but does not remove the issue, particularly in a multi-tenant setting.
finding.source: $_POST['set_webhook'] (import.php:17-19), POST parameter restricted to sessions with is_admin set
finding.sink: curl_init($hook) followed by curl_exec($ch) at import.php:20-22

trace.note: Branch entered when `set_webhook` is present in the POST data.
require_admin() checks $_SESSION['is_admin'] and exits with 403 otherwise. This is the only guard on the path.
$hook is assigned directly from $_POST['set_webhook'] with no sanitisation.
curl_init($hook) sets CURLOPT_URL to the attacker-supplied value.
curl_exec() performs the request from the server's network position. The body is discarded and only 'ok' is echoed back.

finding.guards_checked: require_admin() session check only. There is no scheme or host allowlist, no check of the resolved IP against private or link-local ranges, no CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS or CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS restriction, and no DNS pinning. CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is not set, so redirects are not followed.

verdict.guard_found: require_admin() session check only (import.php:4-9, 18); no URL/host/scheme validation
verdict.reason: The trace matches import.php:17-22, but $_POST['set_webhook'] reaches curl_init at import.php:20 only after require_admin() at import.php:18 passes, so the source is admin-only and not controllable by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker.
